evidence.clarity: 1440: H1 'Security questionnaires drafted from your own policies. Every answer cited or flagged.' plus a lede naming the buyer (enterprise buyers send you) and the approver (your security lead), then 'Request a pilot by email' with 'Opens a blank email to pilots@paperwren.example' directly under it. What, for whom and next step are all said before the fold, and nothing later contradicts them.
evidence.fit: Every ask in the brief is met. The sample runs in the page with nothing uploaded. All three CTAs are mailto:pilots@paperwren.example. Design partners appear unnamed, and accuracy and time saved are shown as 'Not measured yet'. The 'which person first' tension gets a deliberate answer: a four-stage handoff strip (Sales engineer > Paperwren > Security lead > Sales engineer) and then two 'If you're the...' columns, so each role has its own path. The tone is sober and document-like, which suits security reviewers.
evidence.distinctiveness: The page borrows the product's own grammar. The hero lede carries a superscript citation, the pilot facts use the same 'Flagged' chips as the sample, and it ends with 'Notes on this page', each note linking back. Mono section labels ('AGENT LOG', 'SOURCES, FROM YOUR LIBRARY') and paper-and-desk neutrals with one citation blue fit the product. The section skeleton below the hero (numbered steps, 4-up strip, two columns) is more conventional.
evidence.proof: 1440: the sample card sits in the first viewport with the question, agent log and draft answer showing. Operated: switched to the Q 9.1 tab, which shows 'No source in your policies, so nothing was drafted' and names the closest passage it did not use. That answers the 'makes things up' doubt directly. Sources are quoted beside the draft with section numbers, and the card is labelled 'Illustrative: a made-up questionnaire and made-up policies' in its header.
evidence.craft: There is a clear type scale (H1 clamp 36-44, body 17, mono 13), consistent rules and a desk-grey tint for logs and sources, and no overflow at 320, 390, 768 or 1440. Defects: footnote superscripts render at 8.84-11.56px (the '2' in the card header is 8.84px), the 'Owner' kickers are 11px, and during Replay the card holds its height with a large blank white area for about 2s (1440, clicked 'Replay the draft').
evidence.mobile: 390: the phone layout is recomposed, not shrunk. The tabs become stacked full-width rows with the chip on the right, the CTA is full width at 52px, the reviewer buttons split 50/50 at 48px, and nav stays visible as a row with 44px targets. But the sample starts at about y=770, so it only appears in the second screen. The card is long (about 1290px for the Q 9.1 panel), and footnote superscript links are about 13x15px tap targets.
evidence.honesty: The sample is labelled in its own header ('Illustrative... Nothing here is uploaded or sent'), and the reviewer reads 'Priya Natarajan · Security lead (sample)'. The CTA says what happens before you click ('Opens a blank email... Nothing to upload, no call to book'). Small slips: note 5 'Sales engineers tell us the draft changes their work...' is an unattributed anecdote. The pilot aside is close to a list of what the company lacks (Accuracy / Time saved: Not measured yet), though the Flagged chips turn it into the product's own voice.
evidence.interaction: Operated at 1440, 768 and 390. Approve, Send back, Write the answer and Mark not applicable each replace the status chip with its own outcome text in an aria-live region, hide the pair, and offer 'Reset the sample', which restores the state and refocuses. ArrowRight on the tabs switches panels. Replay steps the log in at 420ms and re-enables itself. No console errors. Minor: 'Send back' says 'Returned to drafting with her note' although no note exists, and 'Reset the sample' and 'Replay the draft' are 40px tall.
evidence.copy: The nouns are specific: 'Encryption Standard v3.2 §4.1', 'closest miss', 'mark it not applicable', 'Chasing answers in chat becomes reviewing a list'. Terms stay consistent (cited / flagged / approve / send back). Button labels say what happens. The line 'Every claim above carries a note or a flag, the way an answer should' ties the page to the product. Slightly over-explained in places: the notes section repeats the pilot aside almost word for word.
evidence.first_screen: 1440: promise, named approver, a CTA labelled with its real result, and the sample card's question, log and cited draft all fit in one viewport, which scores 9 at this width. 390: the promise and CTA fit, but nothing backs them until the 'Sample questionnaire' header peeks in at the bottom edge, so the believability is missing at phone width.

evidence.clarity: The H1 'Every answer cites your policy, or it tells you it couldn't.' is a sharp promise but does not say what the product is. The lede supplies that ('drafts replies to the security questionnaires your enterprise buyers send... Your security lead approves every answer'). 'Request a pilot' has an object, and the note under it names the address.
evidence.fit: The demo runs in-page with nothing uploaded, labelled as a fictional vendor's library. The CTA is a well-made pre-filled mailto. Design partners are unnamed and no numbers are claimed. The audience tension is resolved by choosing the security lead ('Written for the person who has to approve it'). The sales engineer gets one aside paragraph, so the second audience has a token line rather than a path.
evidence.distinctiveness: The highlighter idea runs through the page: the yellow bar in the wordmark, yellow citation chips, and yellow marks over the matched policy text. Serif editorial body type sets it apart from SaaS sans. The structure is familiar, though: a headline-led hero, a three-column 'points' grid and a CTA card.
evidence.proof: The artifact is strong once reached. Watched the autoplay at 1440: step 2 highlights the matching sentences in Data Protection Policy §4.1 and Key Management Standard §2.3, step 4 underlines each sentence with 'Matches §4.1', and a 'Needs review: key rotation' flag shows 'No section on rotation.' in the source column. But at 1440 only the step bar shows at the fold (demo top about y=700). Before it scrolls into view the answer column is mostly empty (operator 1440.png shows step 1 with a large blank area). The review step plays itself.
evidence.craft: The serif/sans pairing and highlighter colour are handsome, and the source column beside the draft at 1440 is well composed. Defects: axe reports color-contrast on 12 nodes at 1440 and 8 at 390 (--ink-mute #7a818c on #f3f4ef is about 3.5:1 on the 15px CTA note, the q-meta and 'Draft answer' labels, and the dimmed 0.45-opacity document list). The H1 serif falls back to a default Times-like face in this renderer. The answer column has min-height 520px with large dead space in steps 1-2.
evidence.mobile: 390: some recomposition. Step labels collapse to numbered dots with a 'Step 3 of 5: Draft' line, and the hero stacks cleanly with no overflow. But the top nav is simply hidden (no menu), the step buttons are 34x34px, and the demo starts around the second-to-third screen. The source passages move below the draft, so tapping citation '1' scrolls away from the sentence, and the 'Matches §' check labels are hidden on phones, which weakens step 4.
evidence.honesty: The demo is labelled above it ('This runs on a fictional vendor's policy library... nothing leaves your browser'), and the pilot paragraph is plain about having no figures. But two claims are not in the brief. 'a draft that arrives already checked gets approved in one pass instead of three' is a review-rounds saving stated as fact. 'A person replies, usually the same day' is a response-time promise under the primary CTA.
evidence.interaction: The step buttons jump correctly, Replay restarts, and citation chips pulse the matching mark. But at step 5 the demo approves itself: 'Approved. Added to the questionnaire...' appears without any click. The Approve button has tabindex=-1. Clicking 'Send back' does nothing (the is-approved state stays true and there is no handler). So the 'Your call' step is a picture of a decision, not a control. No reset path for a review choice, no console errors.
evidence.copy: Very good copy: 'Sales wants the questionnaire back by Friday. Security has to stand behind every line of it.' Also 'It won't guess a key rotation period, assume a certification, or borrow an answer from a previous questionnaire you didn't write', plus a pre-filled email asking for company, approver and questionnaires per quarter. It is let down by the unsupported 'one pass instead of three' line.
evidence.first_screen: 1440 and 390: a specific promise and a 'Request a pilot' action are visible. Nothing in view backs the promise: at 1440 only the demo's step bar shows at the fold, and at 390 the demo heading is below the hero. The note under the CTA adds an unsupported 'usually the same day'.

problems: The review step is fake: at step 5 the demo approves itself, Approve is tabindex=-1, and 'Send back' has no effect, which undercuts the brief's core point that the security lead decides

hard_fail_flags.evidence: The 'For the reviewer' section ends with 'For the sales engineer waiting on all this: a draft that arrives already checked gets approved in one pass instead of three.' This is a quantified saving in review rounds (3 to 1), presented as fact and unlabelled. The brief says 'no accuracy or time-saved numbers' and supplies no such figure.
hard_fail_flags.steps: Open packets/P008/B/index.html from disk at any width, scroll to the section headed 'Written for the person who has to approve it', and read the yellow-bordered paragraph (p.aside-note) under the three points.

reason: A puts an operable, clearly labelled artifact in the first screen at 1440. It shows both the cited and the flagged case, and every reviewer control actually changes state and resets. It also gives each of the two audiences a real path. B has the more beautiful highlighter demo and sharper copy, but its review step decides for the visitor, Send back is dead, and it adds a 'one pass instead of three' saving the brief never supplied. I would switch to B only if its review controls worked, the unsupported claims were cut and the demo moved up into the first screen.
